duty.title: “Should” statements — running in shackles
duty.description: In this article, we dive into the world of cognitive distortions, exploring how they affect our perception of reality and mental well-being. We will focus specifically on understanding and correcting “should” statements to help you find a more mindful and balanced outlook on life.

texts: We now understand that our mental state is closely linked to our thinking. In a state of depression, we tend to distort facts, as if looking at the world through gray-tinted glasses: everything seems less vibrant than it would through clear ones.
Depression distorts our ability to see the world objectively, adding layers to our perception that don’t support mental well-being or optimism. Today, we will discuss some of these patterns.
We are talking about cognitive distortions, also known as thinking errors, which are a key element of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).
To understand cognitive distortions, let’s first look at what cognition is. It is the ability to perceive, reason, and process information received through our senses.
Cognition helps us perceive, understand, and remember the world around us, as well as make decisions and solve problems.
In short, cognition is a mental process involving thoughts, images, and representations.
<important>Thus, cognitive distortions are errors in thinking that occur during information processing in the brain, which interfere with logical reasoning.</important>
These are distortions in how we interpret the meaning of what is happening, occurring when a person’s view of reality does not align with the facts or reality itself.
<q author="Aaron Beck">If our thinking is bogged down in distorted symbolic meanings, illogical reasoning, and erroneous interpretations, we become blind and deaf to reality.</q>
In our app, we have highlighted the most important cognitive distortions, which you can explore on their respective pages in the automatic thought journal.
In this course, we will take a detailed look at the three most common errors. We’ll start with “should” statements.
“Should” statements involve rigid beliefs about how things ought or ought not to be. These beliefs create demands placed on yourself, others, and the world.
This distortion is extremely common: we create a rigid model of the world, and when reality doesn’t meet these standards, we experience negative emotions.
Examples of “should” statements:
• I should be liked by everyone
• I shouldn’t make mistakes
• I must be in control of everything
• A man is obligated to provide for his family
• People around me should be attentive and polite

The word “should” implies a lack of alternatives, even though they often exist. “Should” statements create the illusion of a perfect world, and when we step outside of it, we collide with a harsh reality.
This distortion robs us of choice, presenting an ultimatum: either act in a certain way, or experience guilt and other unpleasant emotions.
Why are “should” statements dangerous? With adaptive thinking, the mismatch between expectations and reality doesn’t cause problems because the person understands that not all desires are achievable.
However, with unhelpful thinking, one’s own model of the world carries more weight than reality. The model is perceived as absolute, while reality is seen as flawed.

test.question: Why are cognitive distortions harmful?
answers: They prevent us from perceiving reality objectively
They make it impossible to succeed in life

texts: How can you work with this distortion? The first step is awareness. Watch your thoughts and write them down when they contain words like “should,” “must,” or “have to.” This will help you understand how “should” statements affect your emotions.
The second step is challenging them. Ask yourself: “Why do I believe it has to be this way?” and “What is the evidence that it must be this way?”
The third step is finding alternatives. Replace “should” with “I would like” or “it would be nice.” For example:
• “It would be nice if my partner did what I consider right. But they have the right to their own view of reality.”
• “I would like to be flawless. But I am a human being and it’s okay to be imperfect.”
In conclusion, we invite you to practice identifying and softening “should” statements in your daily life. Start by mindfully observing your thoughts and reactions in various situations.
Pay attention to moments when you tend to use words like “should,” “must,” or “have to,” and ask yourself questions to challenge these automatic thoughts.

guilt.title: The Shadow of Guilt: The Link Between Guilt and Depression
guilt.description: This article explores the connection between guilt and depression, highlighting how excessive or unfounded guilt can contribute to the development of depressive states. We distinguish between helpful and unhelpful guilt, discussing how the former can serve as motivation for positive change, while the latter often leads to self-isolation and deeper depression. You’ll also find strategies for developing self-awareness and addressing unhelpful guilt to improve your mental well-being.

texts: Excessive guilt is often an overlooked symptom of depression, even for many psychologists and psychotherapists.
Nevertheless, excessive guilt is a common symptom of depression, and its intensity is often linked to the severity of the disorder.

<important>Depression accompanied by guilt can convince a person that they are unworthy of life, that they have caused irreparable harm to someone, or that others would be better off without them.</important>
The link between guilt and depression is bidirectional, meaning one can trigger the other.
Frequent experiences of guilt can contribute to the development of a depressive state.
Indeed, it is difficult to maintain a positive emotional state when you’re constantly blaming yourself for everything: your problems, your circumstances, and your relationships.
Such self-criticism, thought patterns, and the accompanying guilt can persist for years, sometimes even a lifetime.
For various reasons, a person may conclude that they failed to handle a situation when they should have, or that they should have acted differently, or felt the situation in another way.
If this conclusion becomes ingrained and guilt becomes a frequent “guest,” a person may develop full-blown depression.
Depression can also be a reaction to “chronic problems.” A person tries to cope with them, but may lack the necessary experience or skills to resolve them.
The person then blames themselves for this and sinks into depression.
So, guilt is an emotion you experience when you have thoughts like these:
• I did something I shouldn’t have (or failed to do something I should have), and this contradicts my moral standards or sense of fairness.
• This “wrong behavior” proves that I am a bad person (or that I have a tendency to cause harm, that my character is flawed, etc.).
Thus, the perception of one’s own “defectiveness” is a primary driver of guilt.
When in a state of depression, a person often experiences guilt, blaming themselves for almost everything: from a lack of energy and motivation to the inability to feel joy or pleasure.
A person may also blame themselves for having depression, viewing it as a sign that they are “wrong” or “broken.”
Sometimes, loved ones may also blame the person, accusing them of laziness or telling them to stop “suffering over nothing,” which only intensifies the depressive state.
<important>Depressive guilt can arise even in situations that do not violate moral norms, making a person feel guilty where no guilt actually exists.</important>
Under the influence of depression, a person may focus only on their mistakes, overlooking their successes and achievements.
This raises a question: is feeling guilt always a bad thing?
The answer is clear: no. Guilt can be helpful, as it helps us recognize and correct mistakes, supports social norms, and maintains social connection.
Guilt serves as a moral compass, closely tied to our conscience.
<q author="Marcus Tullius Cicero">There is no great evil except guilt.</q>
However, when the sense of guilt becomes excessive or unfounded, it begins to negatively impact our emotional and physical well-being.
While helpful guilt motivates us toward positive change, depressive guilt often leads to isolation and withdrawal.
In some cases, it may even drive a person to resort to self-punishment.
To better understand the difference between helpful and unhelpful guilt, let’s look at some examples:
Helpful guilt
A person realizes they acted wrongly. However, they also understand that at the moment, they were unable to do otherwise.
The circumstances at that time did not allow for a different course of action.
For example, they might not have known the action was wrong, might have been overwhelmed by intense emotions, or lacked the experience to foresee the consequences.

<important>In other words, at that moment, they couldn’t have been better than they were. Now, they have changed, they have “seen the light,” and their values have shifted. They feel shame for the mistake and find it painful to realize how they acted in the past.</important>

In this case, you could say the person is being kind to themselves. They understand their past motives and the reasons for their actions, recognizing the circumstances that prevented them from acting differently.

They understand what can be changed to prevent similar events in the future and what cannot be changed because it is outside of their control. This guilt is not dramatic; it is free from self-flagellation.
The experience is sober and measured, though it can still be quite painful. It is, essentially, sincere remorse rooted in humility and acceptance.
Unhelpful guilt
A person also realizes they acted wrongly. But unlike the first case, they believe they could have acted differently at the moment they made the mistake.

<important>They believe they could have overcome their limitations, such as a lack of knowledge, experience, personality traits, or their emotional state at the time. Essentially, this involves a refusal to accept their real and inevitable limitations in that moment.</important>
This results in a heartbreaking thought: “How could I?!!"
How could I fail to meet expectations, fall so low, make mistakes, or lose control over something or someone?

I could have, I had the chance to act differently, but I didn’t. Oh, the horror! It means I’m not in control of myself. That’s impossible—either I just wasn’t trying hard enough, or I’m simply a bad person.
If they believe they could have overcome their circumstances, no reasons are taken into account. If they could, then they could—plain and simple.
The person constantly revisits past events, re-traumatizing themselves over and over again.
By using the following questions, you can easily determine whether your feelings are helpful remorse or self-destructive, unhelpful, distorted guilt.
• Ask yourself the following questions:
• Did I truly do something “bad” or “unfair”? Did I cause harm intentionally and deliberately? Or am I being unreasonably demanding of myself, expecting to be flawless, all-knowing, and all-powerful?
• Am I labeling myself as a bad or disgusting person because of this? Do my thoughts contain cognitive distortions, such as exaggeration, overgeneralization, and so on?
• How realistic is my regret or remorse? Does it stem from an empathetic understanding of the negative consequences of my actions?

incrimination.title: Self-esteem in the Depths of Depression: A Path to Self-Acceptance and Inner Balance
incrimination.description: This article explores how depression affects self-esteem, revealing how negative self-perception intensifies depressive symptoms and hinders a fulfilling life. Through real-life case studies and expert advice, it offers practical steps to overcome self-criticism and strengthen inner harmony. This article serves as a reliable guide for those seeking to build self-confidence and change their lives for the better.

texts: A typical symptom of depression is a tendency toward self-blame, feelings of inadequacy, and a sense of lacking personal value or significance.
People often label themselves as a “failure” or “worthless,” believing they are fundamentally bad.

The more severe the depression, the lower the self-esteem. But you are not alone in this. Research by psychologist Aaron Beck shows that over 80% of people suffering from depression experience feelings of worthlessness.
Your self-image changes significantly during depression: you feel inadequate, overwhelmed, lonely, and deprived. You criticize yourself, your actions, your abilities, and your future.
Self-criticism can take several forms:
• Self-blame — “It’s all my fault”
• Labeling — “I’m so stupid”
• Self-hatred — “I can’t stand myself”
• Self-doubt — “I won’t succeed at anything”

Think about what it’s like to live with such an “appealing” list. At the very least, it’s difficult. When depressed, a person may constantly criticize and belittle themselves without even realizing it.
And, of course, this affects your emotions, mood, and how you view yourself and life in general.
This is why working on your self-esteem is so important. By overcoming self-criticism, you can also influence other symptoms of depression. So, let’s start with your self-esteem.
<q author="Maxwell Maltz">Low self-esteem is like driving through life with the handbrake on.</q>
Low self-esteem acts like a magnifying glass, enlarging every mistake and failure until it feels like a total disaster.
Let’s look at this through a dialogue between a person in depression and a psychologist:
<dialog psy="true">Ekaterina, why did your boss’s remark trigger such intense, negative emotions? Was it really that much of a catastrophe?</dialog>
<dialog>Yes, it was terrible, because I looked like such a fool.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">Let’s assume you did look that way. What does that mean to you?</dialog>
<dialog>It means my boss thought I was stupid.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">And even if he did think that, what follows from it?</dialog>
<dialog>Then I don’t deserve to work at this company.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">And if you truly don’t deserve it, what does that mean?</dialog>
<dialog>It means I’m a worthless person who won’t achieve anything in life and will spend the rest of my days cleaning floors somewhere.</dialog>
This example shows how a small remark from a manager is perceived as proof of Katya’s worthlessness and predicts a bleak future for her.
Thus, when we are in depression, small mistakes are perceived as tragedies. In this state, we are often unable to think realistically or logically.
Instead, we become convinced of our own inadequacy and uselessness. We then convince others of this by vividly demonstrating our flaws and persistently speaking of our failures.

First, it’s important to realize that you cannot earn your worth. Success can certainly bring pleasure, but it doesn’t bring happiness. And self-esteem based solely on achievements is a false sense of self—it isn’t realistic.

Many successful but unhappy people suffering from depression also feel worthless. Evidence of this can be seen in famous figures who seemingly had everything—career, money, fame, and talent—yet they took their own lives.
Most people suffering from depression are actually capable of so much; they can be talented, attractive, and interesting, and they may be surrounded by the love and care of those close to them.
<important>But this doesn’t help them because they lack self-love and self-respect. Only your sense of self-worth determines how you feel.</important>
A very important step toward awareness is paying close attention to what you think and say about yourself.
The next time you insist on your own inadequacy or negatively judge yourself, your actions, or your experiences, try to find real evidence for it. Often, this evidence is irrational and meaningless.
Second, try to replace self-criticism with self-correction.
When you learn something new, like a new language, a teacher doesn’t hit you over the head with a book or call you stupid just because you don’t know a verb tense or a rule.
That would be a bad teacher with an ineffective method. And you likely wouldn’t want—or be able—to learn a new language that way.
Unfortunately, you often become that bad teacher to yourself, criticizing instead of correcting.
<important>So, instead of criticizing, try asking yourself these questions: Is there a better way to do this? How can I make it happen? What else should I learn?</important>
Third, every time you criticize yourself, try to imagine you are criticizing someone else in the exact same way. Would you be as harsh and blunt with others as you are with yourself.
Start holding your loved ones and friends to the same standards. But be as honest as possible. Once you start doing this, you’ll realize just how unfair your criticism actually is.
Your self-esteem is a crucial motivator when setting life goals and achieving them.
With low self-esteem, you underestimate your potential, depriving yourself of the right to be happy.
To change the situation, you need to change your thinking habits and your behavior. Take small steps toward healthy self-esteem by accepting setbacks and noticing even the smallest successes.

We want to support you on this challenging journey, give you hope, and help you choose manageable tasks to focus on. To do this, we will explore several effective techniques in the following chapters.
